title: Only closeness (8:2)
hookLine: Maimonides pictures the world to come without bodies, a life of knowing God
tomorrow: then why does the Torah keep promising rain and harvests?

cards: Physical therapy, week whatever. The knee won't bend, the back complains, the stairs feel taller than they used to. Somewhere in the middle of it, people say things like: well, in heaven I'll get a new one.
Do we bring our bodies? Maimonides has a surprising answer for the world to come, olam haba. There aren't any.

teach.h: NO BODY, NO FOOD, NO DRINK.
teach.b: In the world to come, he writes, there is no body and no bodily form, only the souls of the righteous, without bodies, like the angels. No eating, no drinking, none of what bodies need.

He quotes the sages of the Talmud: in the world to come there is no eating and no drinking, but the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah, the divine presence.

teach.h: THE CROWN IS WHAT THEY KNEW.
teach.b: Then he explains the crown. It isn't gold. It's the knowing they reached in this life.
And to enjoy the radiance means to know and grasp God in a way they couldn't while in a body. So the picture isn't a buffet and a better knee. It's nearness.
Only closeness. Here's what's worth saying at dinner: for Maimonides, the reward for a life of turning toward God isn't more stuff. It's the turning, finally complete.
Jewish thinkers don't all paint it this way; Nachmanides, for one, pictured the world to come with bodies restored.
And Maimonides himself, in other writings, also affirms the resurrection of the dead; how the two fit is a question his readers still ask. The tradition holds the argument open.
What it keeps, across the argument, is where the road ends: near God.

how: Jewish tradition speaks of olam haba, the world to come, in more than one way; Jews study Maimonides' bodiless picture alongside other views, and the resurrection of the dead is named in the daily Amidah prayer.

o: the world to come as souls near God, without bodies
the world to come as this life, healed and restored
the world to come as rest and food without end

p: the knowing they reached in life
knowing God as no body could

s: Maimonides pictures the world to come as an endless feast
no eating, no drinking: the righteous enjoy the radiance of the divine presence.
for Maimonides, the crowns in the sages' saying are knowledge
the crown is the knowing they reached in this life.
every Jewish thinker shares Maimonides' bodiless picture
Nachmanides, for one, pictured the world to come with bodies restored.

games.q: a friend says Maimonides' world to come sounds boring: no food, no bodies, nothing to do. what's his reply?
o: he agrees; it's a smaller, quieter kind of life.
the radiance, knowing God, is the delight; food was for bodies.
there's still food there, just healthier and endless.
games.why: the righteous 'enjoy the radiance': for Maimonides that means knowing God, a pleasure no body could hold.

practice: Close your eyes and let the body be what it is: the ache, the itch, the weight in the chair. Without fighting any of it, bring to mind someone you love being near you, not doing anything, just near.
Stay with that nearness until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Only closeness: Maimonides' picture of the world to come. No bodies, no food; the righteous knowing God.

carryVoice: Hold this one: no body, only closeness, where the reward is nearness itself. Day twenty-two, complete.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 8:2 (no body or bodily form in the world to come; the souls of the righteous like angels; the crowns are knowledge; enjoying the radiance is knowing God)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (no eating or drinking; the righteous sit with crowns and enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah)
Nachmanides, Sha'ar ha-Gemul; Maimonides, Essay on Resurrection
